newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TENNIS-CHANG AND PIERCE STEAL THE LIMELIGHT.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-CHANG AND PIERCE STEAL THE LIMELIGHT.

text.p: World number two Michael Chang charged into the semifinals of the Australian Open for the third successive year on Tuesday and then warned his rivals his best tennis was still to come.
Chang, who has not won a grand slam event since lifting the French Open title eight years ago, ruthlessly disposed of ninth seeded Chilean Marcelo Rios 7-5 6-1 6-4 in just under two hours.

Chang has dropped only one set in his past five matches at Melbourne Park and will next meet another baseliner, Spain's Carlos Moya who continued his run with a four-set victory over 10th seeded compatriot Felix Mantilla.
In the women's event, former champion Mary Pierce of France came from behind to beat Sabine Appelmans of Belgium and South Africa's Amanda Coetzer brushed past American Kimberly Po.
Chang was a beaten finalist here last year and has also been runner-up at the French and U.S. Open in the past two years. But he said he did not did not feel under any pressure.
"I'm not too concerned about whether or not I'm able to win another grand slam title and stuff like that," he said.
"I like to think things are getting better and better...I still feel like my best tennis is ahead of me."
Day-time matches were overshadowed by a row over the tournament referee's decision to pull the roof over Centre Court to spare players and public from a heatwave.
Courtside temperatures at Melbourne Park exceeded 50 degrees Celsius over the weekend, leading to warnings that players could be at risk.

But referee Peter Bellenger's decision to close out the sun provoked an angry reaction among players, coaches and tennis veterans who said Melbourne's fickle weather was part of the tournament's tradition.
"I was going to play anyway so even if it's snowing, raining or 60 degrees (Celsius), I don't care," Moya said after beating Mantilla in four sets.
"I think it may have been a different match in the sun and wind," retorted a furious Mantilla.
Moya had to put friendship aside as he disposed of 14th seedeMantilla 7-5 6-2 6-7 6-2.
Once considered just another Spanish clay-court baseliner, Moya has grown in confidence since ousting defending champion Boris Becker in the first round. On Tuesday he regularly came to the net.
It was Spain's best performance at the Australian Open since Andres Gimeno lost the 1969 final to Australian Rod Laver.
In the first women's quarter-final, Coetzer showed the same form which helped her bring down top seed Steffi Graf as she beat Po 6-4 6-1 in a match lasting 67 minutes.
Coetzer is seen as the player with the best chance of beating Swiss starlet Martina Hingis if both win through to Saturday's final. Her performance on Tuesday must have reinforced that view.
Although Po managed to break Coetzer's serve once in each set, the South African converted six of six break points.
Coetzer also criticised the decision to shut the roof for the day's play, although she conceded it had given herself and Po a break from the heat.
"I definitely would have preferred playing outside...I love playing out in the sun," she said.
Since her victory here in 1995, Pierce has had to cope with a prolonged form slump and a shoulder injury. She took a three-month break from the game late last year.
Pierce lost the first set 6-1 before levelling the match in the second and then came back from 3-0 down in the third to beat Appelmans 1-6 6-4 6-4.
"That's the great thing about tennis, you never know what's going to happen," she said, looking forward to a tough semifinal date with Coetzer.
